steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Film movements are coherent groups of filmmakers who share aesthetic principles, production methods and ideological commitments during a specific historical period.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Italian Neo-Realism emerged after World War II, rejecting studio artificiality in favour of location shooting, non-professional actors and stories about working-class struggle.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The French New Wave of the late 1950s and 1960s challenged mainstream French cinema with location filming, handheld camera, jump cuts and self-reflexive storytelling.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: German Expressionism of the 1920s used distorted set design, exaggerated shadows and stylised performance to convey psychological turmoil and social anxiety in post-World War I Germany.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always identify the specific film movement by name and era rather than making vague references to old or foreign films. Link visual techniques to their historical context: German Expressionism's distortion reflects post-World War I anxiety, not just stylistic preference. Use named films as examples: reference Bicycle Thieves for Neo-Realism, Breathless for the New Wave, The Cabinet of Dr Caligari for Expressionism. Explain how film movements challenged the dominant cinema of their time, not just what their techniques were. Consider how the influence of historical film movements can be seen in contemporary films you have studied.
